recall_prompt: Say how you would do this one — say what [x] equals just below 2, and what x itself does.

page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: Find [x] just below 2
steps.margin_note: First mark. The value of [x] here is 1, not 2. The mark is for that statement together with its interval.
lines: [x] is the greatest integer function: [x] is the greatest integer less than or equal to x.
x → 2⁻ means x takes values slightly less than 2, that is 1 < x < 2.

recall.must_convey: That for 1 < x < 2 the greatest integer function [x] has the constant value 1.
accept: just below two the greatest integer is one
between one and two the floor value is one
x is a little less than two so bracket x is one
two kanna thakkuva unte bracket x equals one
the greatest integer below one point nine nine is one

steps.why: On the interval 1 < x < 2 the greatest integer function is the constant 1. The value at x = 2 itself is never used, because a limit looks only at values near the point.
common_mistakes: Writing [x] = 2 by rounding 1.999 up to the nearer integer.
Using [2] = 2, the value AT the point, which the one-sided limit does not use.
steps.memory_tip: Just below 2 the step up to 2 has not happened yet, so [x] is still 1.

steps.label: Add and take the limit
steps.margin_note: Second mark. Box 3. Only [x] is held at 1; x itself still approaches 2, so the two terms are different numbers.

recall.must_convey: That the expression becomes 1 + x, whose limit as x approaches 2 is 3.
accept: one plus x gives three as x approaches two
the floor part is one and x approaches two so the sum is three
the left hand limit is three
one plus two equals three ani vasthundi

steps.why: Only the integer part is held at 1; x itself still approaches 2, so the sum approaches 1 + 2 = 3.
common_mistakes: Giving 4, which is the RIGHT-hand limit, where [x] = 2.
Writing 1 + 1 by letting x approach 1 as well as the floor value.
steps.memory_tip: Below 2 the pair is 1 from the step and 2 from x, which is 3.
